explanations.explanation: This feature is a detector for user-emphasized words—i.e. tokens surrounded by double-asterisks (bold formatting) that the author has marked as important.

This feature detects tokens that kick off a new block or heading—i.e. the very first word (often a year, keyword, title or section label) at the start of a paragraph, list item, code block, or section header.

This hidden unit is essentially a “document‐structure” detector: it lights up on section and title headings, bylines/author or photo‐credit lines, separator dashes (– or ---), all‐caps metadata (e.g. “FILE –”, “ATTORNEY GENERAL…”), and other formatting cues that mark section breaks or header blocks rather than the body semantics.

This neuron fires on formal label‐words or acronyms that serve as headers or institutional tags in structured text—e.g. degree abbreviations (BA, MBA, MFA), department/discipline names (“Sciences”), and section or category markers (“Services,” “Category”). It flags those multi‐letter, all-caps or title-case tokens that label organizational roles, academic credentials, or document sections.
This feature fires on the first‐person self-reference marker – essentially spotting “I” when it appears as the clause subject, flagging the start of a speaker’s own statement.

The feature is a detector for the discourse marker “case” when used in “in (this/any/such) case,” i.e. it flags the conditional/hypothetical/exemplifying connective that introduces an exception or specific scenario.

This feature marks the typical “file‐header” or document preamble—i.e. the boilerplate block at the top of code or text files (copyright/license notices, comment‐ or markup‐delimiters like /**…*/, //…, <!DOCTYPE>, etc.).
This feature is a detector for Markdown “strong” emphasis markers (the double‐asterisk tokens that begin and end bolded headings or titles).

This feature is a “delimiter” detector: it lights up on tokens that mark or end logical units—sentence‐terminating punctuation (., ?, etc.), line/block comment markers (#, //, ///), section headers, and similar boundary symbols across prose, code, math problems and markdown.

This neuron flags highly structured reference-style metadata: legal docket/case citations, formal license headers, and journal-article identifiers (e.g. volume–issue–page codes in markdown image links).
